title: Spray blocking
subtitle: Lightly dampening a pinned piece to relax the stitches without full immersion.
excerpt: Spray blocking mists a pinned knitted piece with water from a spray bottle and leaves it to dry in shape. It is the gentlest blocking method, well suited to delicate lace, lightweight yarns, and pieces that need only a light set rather than full saturation.
sourceNotes: Standard finishing practice in UK hand-knitting tradition. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) describes damping as the light alternative to full pressing.
heroPrompt: A spray bottle misting water over a lace knitted swatch pinned to a blocking mat, water droplets visible on the yarn.

glossaryTerms.definition: A finishing method in which a knitted piece is pinned to shape and then misted with water from a spray bottle and left to dry in position.

content.text: is the lightest of the three main blocking methods. The piece is pinned to its finished dimensions first, then misted evenly with water from a spray bottle and left to dry. Because the fibres are never saturated, the method suits lightweight lace, mohair blends, and any yarn where full immersion could distort the halo or the drape. It is also the quickest: a spray-blocked piece dries faster than a wet-blocked one. Difficulty: beginner.
A clean spray bottle filled with cold or lukewarm water
A foam blocking mat or clean flat surface that can tolerate moisture
A measuring tape or printed schematic to check dimensions
Lay the finished piece on the blocking mat. Ease it towards the finished dimensions stated in the pattern, using your hands to coax the fabric into shape.
Pin the edges securely, placing pins every 2-3 cm along straight edges and more frequently around curves and lace points. Check measurements with the tape measure.
Hold the spray bottle about 20 cm above the surface and mist the piece evenly. The goal is a light, even dampness, not saturation. Work methodically across the whole piece.
Gently pat the piece flat where needed and re-check the dimensions. Add more pins if any section has shifted.
Leave to dry completely before removing the pins. This typically takes 2-4 hours at room temperature, or overnight for heavier pieces.

Spray blocking suits lace shawls in fine mohair or silk blends. It also works well for colourwork accessories where full immersion might cause colours to run. Use it whenever you want a gentle set without the long drying time of a fully soaked piece. For a gauge swatch, a light spray is enough to relax the fibres before measuring.

items.symptom: Piece has not changed shape or the stitches look the same as before
items.cause: Too little moisture, or a synthetic yarn that does not respond to water
items.fix: Mist more generously, keeping the bottle moving so the whole surface is damp. If the yarn is acrylic, the fibres will not relax with water; the shape must be set while knitting.

items.symptom: Edges have stretched unevenly after drying
items.cause: Pins placed too far apart or removed before the piece was fully dry
items.fix: Add more pins, especially on curved and diagonal edges. Do not unpin until the yarn feels dry to the touch throughout.

items.symptom: The piece smells musty after drying
items.cause: It was left in a damp environment or not allowed to dry fully
items.fix: Always dry in a well-ventilated room. If the smell persists, wet block the piece properly, then dry in fresh air.
